extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners preparing/responding to Office actions)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and form-paragraphs from the MPEP for making and framing rejections under 35 U.S.C. 101 and 103 (including biotech 103(b)), plus procedural requirements and templates for Office actions. Covers statutory citations, Graham factors, provisional rejections, joint ownership/disqualification rules, utility/enablement, and Atomic Energy Act reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double patenting — terminal disclaimer
rubrics_metrics.description: The double patenting rejection may be obviated by filing a terminal disclaimer in accordance with 37 CFR 1.321(d). See MPEP § 804 and § 804.02.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If double patenting is asserted, advise applicant that filing a terminal disclaimer per 37 CFR 1.321(d) can obviate the rejection; cite MPEP §804/§804.02.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of statutory statement for 35 U.S.C. 103(a) (¶ 7.20)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotable statement of 35 U.S.C. 103(a) forms basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute quotation is required in first actions on the merits employing 35 U.S.C. 103(a) and in final rejections; otherwise, when the statute is applied but not cited, use paragraph 7.103. This form paragraph should only be used ONCE in a given Office action and must precede form paragraphs 7.20.01-7.22 when citing the statute in first actions and final rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: 103(a) rejection using 102(e),(f),(g) where reference also qualifies under another 102 subsection (¶ 7.20.01)
rubrics_metrics.description: If applicant shows common ownership or joint research with respect to [1] at the time the invention was made, but the reference additionally qualifies as prior art under another subsection of 35 U.S.C. 102, the reference is not disqualified under 35 U.S.C. 103(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant may overcome the applied art either by a showing under 37 CFR 1.132 that the invention disclosed was derived from the inventor of this application (not 'by another'), or by antedating the applied art under 37 CFR 1.131. Include this form paragraph following 7.20 in actions containing 103(a) rejections using art that is disqualified under 103(c) by 102(e),(f) or (g) but qualifies under another 102 subsection. Identify references in bracketed slots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of common ownership for joint inventors (¶ 7.20.02)
rubrics_metrics.description: When an application names joint inventors, the examiner presumes the subject matter of the various claims was commonly owned at the time inventions were made absent evidence to the contrary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant is advised of the obligation under 37 CFR 1.56 to point out inventor and invention dates for any claim not commonly owned so the examiner can consider applicability of 35 U.S.C. 103(c) and potential 35 U.S.C. 102(e),(f) or (g) prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to provide conspicuous statement for common ownership disqualification (¶ 7.20.04)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant attempted to disqualify reference [1] under 35 U.S.C. 103(c) by showing common ownership/assignment, but failed to provide a statement that the application and the reference were owned by, or subject to an obligation of assignment to, the same person at the time the invention was made in a conspicuous manner; therefore the reference is not disqualified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant must file the required evidence to properly disqualify the reference under 35 U.S.C. 103(c). Also advise applicant of alternatives: showing derivation under 37 CFR 1.132 or antedating under 37 CFR 1.131. Include this paragraph in all actions with 103(a) rejections where an attempt to disqualify under 103(c) was made but was ineffective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint research agreement disqualification requirements (¶ 7.20.05)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant attempted to disqualify reference [1] under 35 U.S.C. 103(c) by showing the invention was subject to a joint research agreement at the time the invention was made, but applicant failed to [2].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant must file the missing requirements (see 37 CFR 1.71(g) and 1.104(c) and MPEP §706.02(l)). Reasons the attempt could be ineffective include noncompliance with statutory requirements of 35 U.S.C. 103(c) or failure to comply with CREATE Act rule requirements (e.g., failure to submit required statement or failure to amend the specification to include the names of the parties to the joint research agreement). Identify the reference and specify reasons in bracketed slots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing a 35 U.S.C. 103(a) rejection — procedural requirements (¶ 7.21)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over [2].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This paragraph must be preceded by form paragraph 7.20 or 7.103. An explanation of the rejection applying the Graham v. Deere test must follow this form paragraph. If reliance is on prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(e), apply AIPA rules to determine prior art date unless the reference is a U.S. patent issued from an international application with filing date prior to November 29, 2000 (use pre-AIPA 102(e) only in the narrow circumstances described). If the applicability of the rejection prevents disqualification under 103(c), follow with form paragraph 7.20.01. Use 7.21.01 for provisional 103(a) rejections based on copending applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional 35 U.S.C. 103(a) rejection for copending application (¶ 7.21.01)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim [1] provisionally rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as obvious over copending Application No. [2] which has a common [3] with the instant application; based upon the earlier effective U.S. filing date of the copending application, it would constitute prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) if published or patented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provisional rejection is based on presumption of future publication/patenting of the copending application. It may be overcome by showings under 37 CFR 1.132 (derivation), 37 CFR 1.131 (date of invention), or by showing the copending application is disqualified under 35 U.S.C. 103(c). Use this paragraph when copending application has earlier U.S. filing date and common assignee or at least one common inventor. Apply AIPA guidance for determining 102(e) dates; do not use this paragraph in applications pending on/after Dec 10, 2004 when copending application is disqualified under 103(c). If the claimed invention is also claimed in the copending application, consider obviousness double patenting using paragraphs 8.33 and 8.37, and other related rejections as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: 103(a) rejection where reference has common assignee or inventor (¶ 7.21.02)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being obvious over [2]; the applied reference has a common [3] with the instant application and constitutes prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) based on its earlier effective filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rejection might be overcome by (1) showing under 37 CFR 1.132 that any invention disclosed but not claimed in the reference was derived from the applicant's inventor; (2) showing an earlier date of invention under 37 CFR 1.131; or (3) filing an oath/declaration under 37 CFR 1.130 stating current common ownership and that the named inventor is the prior inventor under 35 U.S.C. 104, together with a terminal disclaimer under 37 CFR 1.321(c). The reference could also be disqualified under 35 U.S.C. 103(c). Apply AIPA rules for 102(e) date where applicable. Insert --assignee-- or --inventor-- in bracket 3 and explanation of obviousness in bracket 4.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining references — 35 U.S.C. 103(a), further in view (¶ 7.22)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over [2] as applied to claim [3] above, and further in view of [4].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This paragraph must be preceded by form paragraph 7.21. An explanation applying the Graham v. Deere test must follow. If relying on prior art under 102(e), apply AIPA rules to determine reference dates as specified in 7.12/7.12.01 guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham v. Deere test for obviousness (¶ 7.23)
rubrics_metrics.description: The factual inquiries set forth in Graham v. John Deere Co. that are applied for establishing a background for determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103(a): (1) determining the scope and contents of the prior art; (2) ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue; (3) resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art; (4) considering objective evidence present in the application indicating obviousness or nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An explanation applying Graham must follow 103(a) rejections. Use these four factual inquiries as the framework for the rationale of obviousness rejections and for responding to applicant arguments invoking Graham.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to use combined 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103(a) rejection (¶ 7.27)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102([2]) as anticipated by or, in the alternative, under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as obvious over [3].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This paragraph is NOT intended to be commonly used as a substitute for a single appropriate rejection; use a single rejection under 102 or 103 when possible. Circumstances where this paragraph may be used include: (a) claim interpretation dispute where one interpretation supports 102 and another supports 103; (b) reference discloses all limitations except a property or function and examiner cannot determine inherent possession (In re Fitzgerald); (c) genus discloses small genus placing claimed species in public possession (In re Schaumann); (d) product-by-process issues where product appears same though produced by different process (In re Marosi, In re Thorpe); (e) means-plus-function/equivalency uncertainty (see §§2183-2184); (f) overlapping ranges where reference lacks specific example within claimed range (Ex parte Lee). If claim interpretation renders claims indefinite, consider 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph. A full explanation should follow this form paragraph. Precede by appropriate form paragraphs (7.07 and 7.08–7.14, 7.20 or 7.103).

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 103(b) applicability for biotechnological processes (706.02(n))
rubrics_metrics.description: Notwithstanding subsection (a), a biotechnological process using or resulting in a composition of matter that is novel under 102 and nonobvious under 103(a) shall be considered nonobvious under 103(b) if: (A) claims to the process and composition are in same application or separate applications having same effective filing date; and (B) the composition and the process at the time invented were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 103(b) precludes rejection of process claims that involve using/making certain nonobvious biotechnological compositions under 103(a). Additional statutory requirements: (C) a patent issued on the process must also contain claims to the composition used/made by the process, or if composition is claimed in another patent, the patents expire on same date; (D) the biotechnological process must fall within statutory definition; (E) a timely election to proceed under 103(b) must be made. See below for definition and election procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'biotechnological process' for 35 U.S.C. 103(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of paragraph (1), 'biotechnological process' means: (A) a process of genetically altering or otherwise inducing a single- or multi-celled organism to (i) express an exogenous nucleotide sequence, (ii) inhibit/augment/alter expression of an endogenous nucleotide sequence, or (iii) express a specific physiological characteristic not naturally associated with the organism; (B) cell fusion procedures yielding a cell line that expresses a specific protein (e.g., monoclonal antibody); (C) a method of using a product produced by a process defined by (A) or (B), or a combination of (A) and (B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 103(b) is applicable to biotechnological processes only. Use this statutory definition to determine whether a process falls within 103(b). See MPEP §2116.01 and Federal Circuit cases (In re Ochiai, In re Brouwer) for further guidance; reliance on 103(b) should be rare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Election procedure for 35 U.S.C. 103(b) treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: An election to proceed under 35 U.S.C. 103(b) shall be made by way of petition under 37 CFR 1.182. The petition must establish that all the requirements set forth in 35 U.S.C. 103(b) have been satisfied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An election will normally be timely if made no later than the earlier of payment of the issue fee or filing of an appeal brief in an application containing a composition claim which has not been rejected under 102 or 103. In certain historical situations (apps pending on/after Nov 1, 1995 with issue fee paid prior to Mar 26, 1996) other timeliness criteria may apply (37 CFR 1.312(b)). If a patent is granted without an election due to error without deceptive intent, a reissue may be filed to permit consideration of qualifying process claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize prior-art-based examination; develop non-prior-art rejections fully (706.03)
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary object of examination is to determine whether claims are patentable over the prior art; this should not be relegated while undue emphasis is given to nonprior art or 'technical' rejections. Effort should be concentrated on truly essential matters, minimizing/eliminating effort on technical rejections which are not critical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a major technical rejection is proper (e.g., lack of proper disclosure, undue breadth, utility), state the rejection with a full development of reasons rather than a mere conclusion with stereotyped language. If using form paragraphs in an office action, incorporation reduces chance of misunderstanding as to grounds of rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. 101 (706.03(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject matter of the invention must come within statutory boundaries of 35 U.S.C. 101: 'any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'process' (35 U.S.C. 100) includes process, art or method, and includes a new use of a known process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter, or material. Use MPEP §§2105–2107 for further guidance on patent eligibility of living subject matter and subject matter eligibility in general. Examples of nonstatutory subject matter include printed matter (mere arrangement of printed matter), naturally occurring articles substantially unaltered, and scientific principles divorced from tangible structure. Use form paragraphs 7.04–7.05.03 to reject under 35 U.S.C. 101.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of statutory basis for 35 U.S.C. 101 (¶ 7.04)
rubrics_metrics.description: Insert the text of 35 U.S.C. 101 in office actions where 101 is used: 'Whoever invents or discovers any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof, may obtain a patent therefor, subject to the conditions and requirements of this title.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This paragraph must precede the first use of 35 U.S.C. 101 in all first actions on the merits and final rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection heading and following specificity (¶ 7.05)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the heading 'Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 because' — this heading-only paragraph must be followed by one of form paragraphs 7.05.01–7.05.03 or another appropriate reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain the rejection following recitation of the statute and use the appropriate specific subparagraph(s). This paragraph must be preceded by form paragraph 7.04 in first actions and final rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-statutory subject matter grounds for 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection (¶ 7.05.01)
rubrics_metrics.description: The claimed invention is directed to non-statutory subject matter because [1].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In bracket 1, explain why the claim is not patent eligible, e.g., (a) why it does not fall within at least one of the four statutory categories; (b) why the claim is directed to a judicial exception (abstract idea, natural phenomenon, law of nature) and is not directed to a practical application (e.g., lacks physical transformation or useful, concrete, tangible result); or (c) why the claim would impermissibly cover every substantial practical application of, and preempt all use of, an abstract idea, natural phenomenon, or law of nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility requirement under 35 U.S.C. 101 (¶ 7.05.02)
rubrics_metrics.description: The claimed invention lacks patentable utility. [1]
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In bracket 1, provide explanation of lack of utility. See MPEP §§706.03(a) and 2105–2107.03 for supporting guidance and law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inoperative invention — lack of utility (¶ 7.05.03)
rubrics_metrics.description: The disclosed invention is inoperative and therefore lacks utility. [1]
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In bracket 1, explain why the invention is inoperative. Use this paragraph where disclosure demonstrates inoperability that defeats patentable utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility rejections under 35 U.S.C. 101 and enablement under 35 U.S.C. 112 (¶ 7.05.04)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 because the claimed invention is not supported by either a [2] asserted utility or a well established utility. Claim [4] also rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, where the specification would not enable one skilled in the art to make or use the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the specification would not enable one skilled in the art, or other reasons support an enablement rejection, make a separate 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph rejection using the Wands factors (In re Wands) and an undue experimentation analysis (see MPEP §§2164–2164.08(c)). Use Format A, B, or C as appropriate: Format A insert '--specific and substantial--' for lack of asserted utility; Format B insert '--credible--' for lack of credible asserted utility; Format C for multiple utilities where none are 'specific and substantial' or 'credible' — insert combined wording and address each utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Atomic Energy Act limitations and reporting (706.03(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 151(a) of the Atomic Energy Act: 'No patent shall hereafter be granted for any invention or discovery which is useful solely in the utilization of special nuclear material or atomic energy in an atomic weapon.' Sections 151(c) and (d) require certain pending applications be reported to the Department of Energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under 37 CFR 1.14(d), applications that disclose or appear to disclose inventions relating to atomic energy are reported to the Department of Energy and the Department will be given access to such applications; such reporting does not constitute a determination that the subject matter is useful or falls within categories specified by the Atomic Energy Act. Use MPEP §706.03(b) for further procedures.
